items.summary: Senior Advocate Shashank Garg on Thursday called for the appointment of arbitrators to be taken away from parties and entrusted to courts or arbitral institutions. Garg said institutional appointments would ensure that arbitrators did not owe their positions to parties or law firms. He acknowledged that the proposal would curtail party autonomy and require further deliberation. “ Take party autonomy away from the appointment process. Let arbitrators be appointed either by the court or by institutions so that arbitrators do not have any masters, so to say. They have no allegiance to firms and no interest arising from who appointed them. The State’s faith in arbitration can then probably be restored, ” he said. “ Half of our problems will go if the appointment of arbitrators is taken away from the parties and is done in an institutional manner. Of course, it is not something that we can move towards right away. It would require a lot more thought and debate. But if we are able to bring this significant change, it will impact us in a very positive way ,” Garg added. He was speaking at a panel discussion during Singapore Convention Week 2026 on whether India’s infrastructure dispute-resolution system was keeping pace with the country’s economic ambitions. The session was held at Maxwell Chambers and was organised by JSA, the International Arbitration and Mediation Centre, the Arbitration Bar of India, White & Case and Osborne Partners. The panel was moderated by JSA Partner Ananya Kumar . The panel comprised Garg, White & Case Partner Aditya Singh , Advocate Divya Adepu and Ishani Vora , Principal and Head of India Disputes at Osborne Partners. items.title: Bombay HC closes taxi drivers' PIL against Marathi rule after State extends deadline by 1 year
items.summary: The Bombay High Court was on Saturday informed by the Maharashtra Transport Department that auto and taxi drivers across the State have been granted a one-year extension to learn, read and speak Marathi. [Mohammed Kasim Ahmed v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] In light of this development, a division bench of Acting Chief Justice Ravindra V Ghuge and Justice Gautam A Ankhad disposed of a public interest litigation (PIL) petition challenging the State government’s notification which made working knowledge of the Marathi language mandatory for rickshaw and taxi drivers across the state. They met the Chief Minister and their photographs were published in the newspapers,” ACJ Ghuge said. The Court directed the government pleader to obtain explicit instructions from the Transport Commissioner on whether a formal policy decision has been finalised on the same. The government counsel informed the Court that a positive policy decision of extension has been taken. “The Government Pleader has taken instructions from the State Transport Commissioner of the State of Maharashtra to communicate to the Court that the time for learning, reading and speaking Marathi language by all rickshaw and taxi drivers is extended for a period of one year, and they are expected to master the language within one year,” the Court order recorded. In view of the extension granted by the State, the High Court concluded that the matter did not warrant further judicial intervention and accordingly disposed of the petition. items.title: Nation wants to know why FIR was registered: Arnab Goswami, Amit Malviya argue in Karnataka High Court
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court on Saturday said it will pass orders on September 3 on petitions filed by former BJP IT Cell head Amit Malviya and Republic TV Editor-in-Chief Arnab Goswami seeking to quash an FIR registered against them on a Congress leader’s complaint [Amit Malviya v State of Karnataka, Arnab Goswami v State of Karnataka]. During a brief hearing today, Justice M Nagaprasanna was amused at a submission made by the Senior Advocate Aruna Shyam who was representing the petitioners. "Short point for consideration, how an FIR can be filed in these kinds of cases, the nation wants to know?," Shyam submitted. items.title: Not a good sign when bar council does not earn respect of its members: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna
items.summary: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna on Saturday that bar councils must introspect on their role in upholding professional ethics, morality and competence. "The Bar Councils, whether the Central or the States, must introspect their role and importance in upholding professional ethics, morality and professional competence. When a Bar Council does not earn the respect of its members, it is not a good sign for the legal profession," she said. Justice Nagarathna made these observations while delivering an address at the 13th convocation of National Law University, Delhi on August 29, 2026. Also present were Delhi High Court Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya, who is Chancellor of the University, judges of the Delhi High Court and Vice-Chancellor Prof GS Bajpai. Her remarks come weeks after a controversy involving Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra, who had directed state bar councils not to enrol the graduating 2026 batch of NALSAR, Hyderabad as advocates after they objected to the invitation of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant for their own convocation. BCI halts enrolment of NALSAR 2026 batch students over campaign against CJI Surya Kant She added that the Bar in India "must rise and speak in a singular voice as to how it could sustain the system of justice dispensation in India," pointing to pendency, delays, rising costs and uncertainty in the system. On the independence of the bar, Justice Nagarathna said, "The independence of the bar is not an entitlement given to lawyers for their own benefit. It exists because a constitutional democracy requires a body of professionals who can advise, argue, challenge and represent without having to ask the permission of the State, the market, or even their own clients before doing so." She also cautioned that any lapse or errors of the bar will have a deep impact on our political and civic life and urged lawyers to change their mindset and endure to work for their clients as a public service, lest they lose their relevance in the future to come. On the legal profession more broadly, she said, "A profession is not an occupation or a trade but an office of trust and cannot be reduced to a person who sells legal knowledge by the hour." She closed her address by telling the graduating batch that they leave the institution as "Officers of the Court and Stewards of the Constitution".

"The police constable of the Whitefield Police Station gets concerned about the imaginary disharmony overnight and alleges such disharmony to be because of the post of the petitioner calling it a victory for Hindu unity," the judge said. Pertinently, the Court said that the Whitefield police was following a pattern of sending notices to accused persons asking them to appear before the police for questioning and then arresting them before they comply with deadline mentioned in the notice. "The Whitefield Police Station appears to have been violating the law time and again as this Court has repeatedly coming across this violation of law from this Police Station. A notice indicating the later date of appearance, appears to have been used to take the petitioner into custody 3 days prior to the fixed date itself. This has been the modus operandi of the policeman who man the Whitefield Police Station," the Court said. Justice M Nagaprasanna Justice Nagaprasanna had earlier this week slammed the Whitefield police in a separate case in which it had resorted to the same modus operandi. In that case, the judge had declared the arrest of a man to be illegal and imposed costs of ₹3 lakh on the police. items.title: SCCA, GCAI sign MOU to boost India-Singapore legal cooperation

The programme is intended to give local and international students practical exposure to in-house legal practice, including legal technology and artificial intelligence, negotiation and forensic investigations. The programme will also involve experienced in-house counsel and industry experts, allowing students to gain first-hand insight into the skills and challenges facing modern legal teams. The two associations will also explore ways to advance professional standards for in-house counsel and promote greater alignment of those standards across jurisdictions. items.summary: Noah saved for the Great Flood. Manu prepared for the deluge. Joseph stored grain for seven years of famine. And then there is our Prime Minister- Narendra Modi. By the end of 2024–25, the PM CARES fund had a closing balance of ₹8,452 crore. During that financial year, it spent just ₹87.85 lakh. That’s 0.01% spent. 0.01. So, what exactly is all that money being saved for? A disaster of biblical proportions that perhaps only the PM knows about? Because, honestly, nothing else explains it. If you follow the news, you probably know this by now. After a long delay, the receipts and payments of the PM CARES Fund for 2023–24 and 2024–25 were finally released. And what do they show? That PM CARES hardly spent any money and transferred 93% of its money into fixed deposits. But the real story of PM CARES is not just that it barely spent money. It is much more dubious. It is about staying away from scrutiny. It is about taking foreign donations. It is about having no stated policy on how much has to be kept in reserves. She sourced a letter written by this Japanese multinational company. to a Ministry of External Affairs official, offering help to COVID-hit people in India. The letter said, “We would like to support such people, provide daily commodities such as food & water.” Sounds normal, right? Help from anyone was welcome at that time. But the letter ended with these lines- “In addition, our Indian factory got approval for restarting production activity in Maharashtra yesterday. items.title: Telangana CM Revanth urges ECI to extend SIR claims window, flags risk of disenfranchisement
items.summary: Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy on Friday, August 28, wrote to Chief Election Commissioner (CEO) Gyanesh Kumar, urging the Election Commission to extend the claims and objections period under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, amid concerns that the exercise could leave a large number of eligible voters out of the final rolls. In his letter, CM Revanth said the verification process had placed particular stress on voters classified as “permanently shifted”. He cautioned that ordinary mobility, temporary absence and relocation for work or marriage should not become grounds for disenfranchisement. According to the data furnished by the EC, Telangana had 3.38 crore electors as on June 10. Of these, 73.39 lakh entries, or 21.7%, have been classified under the Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate (ASDD) categories. Of the 2.65 crore enumeration forms digitised so far, 60.50 lakh have been flagged for anomalies and 32.36 lakh for lack of a link to the previous electoral roll. Revanth said the two categories were distinct and together covered 92.86 lakh electors who would be required to respond to notices. He expressed particular concern over the ASDD list, noting that 45.19 lakh of the 73.39 lakh entries, nearly 62%, had been classified as “permanently shifted”. The Chief Minister said the current methodology did not distinguish between temporary absence and permanent relocation. He also said genuine voters who had moved to another address were not being adequately assisted in enrolling at their new residence, while their names could be deleted from the previous roll. He further raised concerns about the notice process, arguing that deletions under the “shifted” category did not receive the same formal notice mechanism as cases involving data anomalies or unmapped entries. “This may result in eligible citizens discovering that they have been disenfranchised only when they reach the polling booth,” the letter said. Revanth also pointed to the uneven distribution of the SIR workload. Hyderabad, Medchal-Malkajgiri and Rangareddy account for about a third of Telangana’s electors but, according to the figures cited in the letter, account for 58.6% of ASDD entries and 41.9% of verification notices. The Chief Minister said the high level of mobility in these urban districts, where short-term tenancies and frequent movement for employment are common, made it especially difficult for voters to maintain continuous proof of residence.
